nodes.title: Chairman’s Lettter
nodes.summary: The Chairman’s letter to shareholders highlights Bajaj Auto’s record financial performance in FY2025, with revenue crossing ₹50,000 crore (up 12%), EBITDA of ₹10,101 crore (up 14%, margin 20.2%), PBT of ₹11,052 crore, and PAT of ₹8,151 crore (up 9%, or 12% adjusting for a one-time tax provision). Free cash flow was ~₹6,500 crore, with a surplus cash balance of ~₹17,000 crore, despite investments in subsidiaries and capex, and over ₹2,200 crore returned via dividends. The letter details operational milestones: domestic revenue highs, Pulsar’s ₹15,000 crore revenue, the launch of the world’s first CNG motorcycle (Freedom 125), KTM/Triumph growth, record commercial vehicle volumes, Chetak’s leadership in electric scooters, and a strong export recovery led by Latin America. It covers electric vehicle revenue of over ₹5,500 crore (~20% of domestic sales) and leadership in electric two- and three-wheelers. Consolidated results were impacted by losses from Pierer Mobility/KTM restructuring, while subsidiaries Bajaj Auto Credit and Bajaj Do Brasil showed progress. Organizational initiatives include TPM awards and Project Velocity’s 4S framework. The letter also outlines future priorities: reviving domestic momentum, accelerating exports, scaling Chetak and electric three-wheelers, and investing in growth enablers.

nodes.title: Management Discussion and Analysis
nodes.summary: The Management Discussion and Analysis section covers India's macroeconomic outlook, including IMF GDP growth estimate, inflation, RBI repo rate cut, current account deficit, and Union Budget tax rebate, followed by Bajaj Auto's record FY2025 financial performance. It details domestic motorcycles (industry growth, 125cc+ focus, Freedom CNG launch, market share pressure, Pulsar milestone), domestic three-wheelers (ICE decline, EV growth, GoGo launch), electric two-wheelers (Chetak growth, new series, network expansion), and international business (export volumes, regional performance, CV leadership). Outlook addresses restoring 125cc+ competitiveness, GoGo expansion, Chetak sales, export recovery, KTM/Triumph launches, margin pressures, risks and opportunities via Enterprise Risk Management, internal controls (IFC, COSO, ICAI), and R&D innovations (CNG motorcycle, Chetak 35 Series, GoGo range, CV engine upgrades, OBD2B compliance, new models). Operations cover TPM principles, robotics, JIPM award, vendor and dealer TPM, plant capacities, employee strength, HR initiatives, and CSR programs (BEST, BMS, STEP). Employee recognition includes awards and engagement activities, with CSR skilling details. Financial statements include standalone P&L, key ratios, subsidiary details, segment revenue/results, and a cautionary statement.

nodes.title: Management Discussion and Analysis (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers India's macroeconomic outlook, noting IMF's 6.5% GDP growth estimate for FY2025 and FY2026, moderating inflation (WPI below 4%, CPI-IW 2-4%, CPI-AL slightly above 4%), and the RBI's 25 bps repo rate cut to 6%. It mentions the current account deficit at 1.1% of GDP in Q3 FY2025 and the Union Budget 2025's tax rebate threshold increase from ₹7 lakh to ₹12 lakh, expected to boost disposable income and personal mobility demand. It then highlights Bajaj Auto's record FY2025 financial performance: total operating income ₹50,010 crore (up 11.9%), EBITDA ₹10,101 crore (up 14.5%), PBT ₹11,052 crore (up 12.5%), and PAT ₹8,151 crore (up 9% after a one-time exceptional charge of ₹211 crore). Operating EBITDA margin was 20.2%, up 40 bps. Surplus cash stood at ₹16,999 crore after CAPEX, strategic investments, and dividends. The Board recommended a final dividend of ₹210 per share, totaling ₹5,864 crore (72% payout). A chart shows revenue, EBITDA, margin, and PAT trends from FY2019 to FY2025.

nodes.title: Domestic Motorcycles
nodes.summary: The text covers the domestic motorcycle industry's 5% growth in FY25 to 12.25 million units and Bajaj Auto's performance as shown in Table 1. It details the focus on the 125cc+ segment with brands like Pulsar, Dominar, KTM, Husqvarna, and Triumph, and the launch of the Freedom CNG bike targeting 100-110cc riders with ~50% operating cost savings. It mentions market share pressure in the second half and subsequent product and pricing interventions. Table 1 provides domestic motorcycle sales and growth data for 2022-2025, including market size, Bajaj's sales, growth rates, and market share. Key highlights include record domestic revenue on the 125cc+ segment, Pulsar crossing ₹10k crores domestically, Freedom becoming a ₹500 crores brand in 5 months, KTM-Triumph selling ~1 lakh units, KTM's momentum with new models, and Triumph's >60% YoY sales growth aided by network expansion to 136 showrooms and new products.

nodes.title: Domestic Three-Wheelers
nodes.summary: The text covers domestic three-wheeler performance, noting a 4% ICE industry decline and Bajaj Auto's 7% decline, offset by 376% EV growth versus the industry's 59%. It includes Table 2 with detailed sales numbers and market shares for passenger and goods carriers across total, ICE, and EV three-wheelers for FY2023–FY2025. Key highlights mention record commercial vehicle volumes and revenues exceeding ₹10K crores, ICE leadership with 75% market share, EV volumes up 4x and market share trebling, and the 'GoGo' brand launch with 850+ dealerships to drive future growth.

nodes.title: Electric Two-Wheeler
nodes.summary: The electric two-wheeler industry grew over 20% this year, with Bajaj Auto leading through innovation, strong products, and network expansion. Domestic sales data for Chetak EV from 2022 to 2025 shows growth rates of 487%, 343%, 219%, and 125%, reaching 260,033 units. Key highlights include Chetak becoming the #1 electric scooter with volumes more than doubling and market share up 900 bps YoY, the December launch of the Chetak 35 series with best-in-class range, enhanced storage, faster charging, and an affordable variant, and rapid network expansion to over 4,000 touchpoints driving leadership.

nodes.title: International Business
nodes.summary: The text provides an overview of Bajaj Auto's international business performance, focusing on export volumes and revenues from FY22 to FY25. It notes peak exports in FY22 due to post-COVID liquidity, followed by declines in FY23 and FY24 caused by macroeconomic challenges like currency fluctuations and FX shortages. FY25 marked a recovery with total export volumes rising to 1.86 million units (13.9% growth) and double-digit revenue growth, with exports constituting 33.7% of sales. Breakdowns show growth in motorcycles and commercial vehicles, with regional highlights: LATAM achieved record motorcycle sales; Asia and Latin America grew 51% and 30% respectively; Pulsar, Dominar, and CT models saw significant increases; Triumph models are exported to 17 countries. Commercial vehicles maintained leadership in 11 of 12 key countries, with Asia and West Africa growing 50% and 58%, and specific countries showing volume and market share gains. Table 4 provides yearly export volume and value data.

nodes.title: Outlook
nodes.summary: The text outlines Bajaj Auto's outlook, focusing on restoring competitiveness in the 125cc+ motorcycle segment, expanding the GoGo electric three-wheeler brand, increasing Chetak sales, sustaining export recovery, and launching KTM and Triumph products, while managing margin pressures. It discusses risks and opportunities, emphasizing a dynamic external environment and the Enterprise Risk Management framework to mitigate threats and capture opportunities. The internal control system is detailed, covering the IFC framework, annual assessments, alignment with COSO and ICAI, independent testing, and statutory auditors' evaluations. Research and Development is highlighted as central to strategy, with innovations including the world's first CNG motorcycle (Freedom), the Chetak 35 Series electric two-wheeler with floorboard battery, the GoGo electric three-wheeler range, CV engine upgrades from 2V to 4V with ISG and IDSS, OBD2B compliance, and new Pulsar, KTM, and Triumph models with advanced features.

nodes.title: Operations
nodes.summary: Bajaj Auto's operations leverage TPM principles across manufacturing, vendors, dealers, and international distributors to achieve productivity, quality, and cost efficiency. The company uses robotics and automation for flexible production. In FY2025, its Waluj plant received a JIPM TPM award, and two vendors were honored, bringing total award-winning vendors to 37. TPM extends to 1,217 Indian dealerships and 24 international distributor plants. The document also details plant-wise capacities, employee strength (7,444, with 618 women), and HR initiatives focused on talent attraction, skill building, leadership, innovation, and employee engagement. CSR initiatives include BEST, BMS, and STEP programs for skilling youth and technicians.

nodes.title: Statement Of Cash Flows
nodes.summary: The section presents the Statement of Cash Flows for Bajaj Auto Ltd for years ended 31 March 2025 and 2024, covering operating, investing, and financing activities, followed by notes to standalone financial statements. nodes.title: I. Operating activities

nodes.title: A. Property, plant and equipment
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting policies for property, plant, and equipment: capital work in progress at cost net of impairment; PPE (except land) at historical cost less depreciation, freehold land at cost; cost includes directly attributable expenses, replacement parts, and major inspections with separate depreciation for significant parts, while other repairs are expensed; capitalized manufacturing/construction costs reduce expenses; land/buildings held for rental or capital appreciation are investment property; derecognition on disposal or no future benefits with gain/loss in profit and loss; and annual review of residual values, useful lives, and depreciation methods with prospective adjustments.

nodes.title: B. Depreciation and amortisation methods, estimated useful lives and residual value
nodes.summary: The text outlines depreciation and amortisation policies: leasehold land premiums amortised over lease periods; tangible assets depreciated on a pro rata straight-line basis over estimated useful lives, with detailed asset class lives (e.g., buildings 3-60 years, plant and machinery 10-15 years). It covers component depreciation for shorter-life components, use of useful lives differing from Schedule II based on technical assessment, pro rata depreciation for additions, and depreciation up to disposal month. Intangible assets with finite lives are amortised over useful economic life and reviewed for impairment. Technical know-how acquired is amortised over estimated useful life, while internally developed know-how is recognised if future benefits are probable and costs reliably measurable, amortised generally over three years from commercial production. Derecognition gains/losses are recognised in profit and loss.

nodes.title: C. Research and development costs
nodes.summary: The section covers accounting policies for research and development costs and financial instruments. R&D costs are expensed unless development criteria are met, then capitalized and amortized. Investment property is initially at cost, depreciated, and derecognized on disposal. Investments in subsidiaries and associates are at cost less impairment. Financial assets are classified by business model and contractual cash flows into fair value (FVTPL or FVTOCI) or amortized cost. Initial measurement is at fair value plus transaction costs (except FVTPL), with trade receivables exceptions. The SPPI test determines classification. Subsequent measurement depends on category: amortized cost using effective interest method, FVTOCI for equity investments with irrevocable election, and FVTPL for others. Impairment uses expected credit losses, and derecognition occurs when rights expire or risks/rewards transfer. Reclassification is only upon business model change.

nodes.title: C. Research and development costs (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies: research and development costs are expensed unless development criteria are met, then capitalized and amortized; investment property is initially at cost, depreciated, and derecognized on disposal; investments in subsidiaries and associates are at cost less impairment; other financial assets are classified by business model and contractual cash flows into fair value or amortized cost, with initial measurement at fair value plus transaction costs (except FVTPL), subsequent measurement based on SPPI test and business model, including amortized cost criteria.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies for Financial Assets: Classification and Measurement
nodes.summary: This page outlines the Company's accounting policies for other investments and financial assets, covering classification and measurement. It details initial recognition categories: fair value (through OCI or P&L) and amortized cost, based on business model and contractual cash flows. Initial measurement is at fair value, including transaction costs for assets not at FVTPL, with exceptions for trade receivables under Ind AS 115. The SPPI test determines amortized cost or FVTOCI classification. Subsequent measurement depends on business model and cash flow characteristics, with three categories mentioned.

nodes.title: Subsequently measured at amortised cost:
nodes.summary: The text outlines the amortised cost measurement criteria for financial assets under Ind AS 109, requiring a business model to collect contractual cash flows and cash flows that are solely payments of principal and interest (SPPI). It lists examples like debentures, bonds, and trade receivables, and details subsequent measurement using the effective interest rate method, including treatment of premiums, fees, interest income, impairment losses, and derecognition gains/losses. It then specifies conditions for fixed maturity plans (FMPs) to be measured at amortised cost based on intent to hold to maturity, SPPI fulfillment, and negligible churn, failing which they are measured at FVTPL. Finally, it explains that open-ended target maturity funds (ETFs) are held to maturity under a passive buy-and-hold strategy and are assessed to meet SPPI requirements.

nodes.title: Subsequently measured at FVTOCI:
nodes.summary: The text outlines the subsequent measurement of equity investments under Ind AS 109 at FVTOCI. It states that all equity investments are measured at fair value, with held-for-trading equity instruments classified as FVTPL. For other equity instruments, the Company may make an irrevocable election on an instrument-by-instrument basis at initial recognition to present subsequent fair value changes in OCI. Equity instruments in the FVTOCI category are initially and subsequently measured at fair value, with fair value movements recognized in OCI. All fair value changes, excluding dividends, are recognized in OCI, with no recycling to profit and loss even on sale, though cumulative gain or loss may be transferred within equity.

nodes.title: Subsequently measured at FVTPL:
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting policies for financial instruments: measurement at FVTPL for assets not meeting amortised cost or FVTOCI criteria, with gains/losses in profit or loss; impairment of financial assets using forward-looking expected credit losses (ECL), including the simplified approach for trade receivables and low credit risk simplification for debt instruments at FVTOCI; definition and recognition of ECL, including lifetime ECL and presentation in financial statements; grouping of instruments for credit risk assessment; write-off criteria; derecognition of financial assets when rights expire or substantially all risks and rewards are transferred; and reclassification of financial assets only upon a change in business model, applied prospectively without restating prior gains or losses.

nodes.title: C. Financial liabilities
nodes.summary: The section on financial liabilities covers initial recognition at fair value and subsequent measurement at amortized cost, including trade payables and bank borrowings. It details derivative and hedging activities, including hedge accounting for foreign exchange cash flow hedges, treatment of effective and ineffective portions, forward and option contracts, and hedge discontinuation. It also addresses impairment of non-financial assets, foreign currency transactions, inventory valuation, employee benefits (privilege leave, gratuity, provident fund), taxation (income tax, GST, provisions, contingent liabilities, leases), government grants and incentives, dividends, cash and cash equivalents, earnings per share, segment reporting, borrowing costs, fair value measurement, other income, share-based payment arrangements (ESOPs, treasury shares, events after reporting period), changes in accounting policies, and property, plant and equipment.

nodes.title: 7 Derivative and hedging activities
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies: financial liabilities are initially recognized at fair value, subsequently at amortized cost, including trade payables and bank borrowings. Derivative and hedging activities detail recognition at fair value, hedge accounting for foreign exchange cash flow hedges, treatment of effective and ineffective portions, forward and option contracts, and hedge discontinuation. Impairment of non-financial assets is assessed when indicators exist, with recoverable amount as higher of fair value less costs and value in use. Foreign currency transactions are recorded at initial rates, monetary items revalued at closing rates, with gains/losses in profit or loss. Inventories are valued at lower of cost (weighted average) and net realizable value, excluding immaterial machinery spares. Employee benefits include privilege leave as a liability, with short-term portion measured based on expected utilization.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies: Impairment, Foreign Currency, and Inventories
nodes.summary: This page outlines three accounting policies from the notes to standalone financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025. Section 8 covers impairment of non-financial assets, including testing triggers, recognition of impairment loss, recoverable amount determination (higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use), discounting future cash flows, cash-generating units, and recognition in profit or loss. Section 9 addresses foreign currency transactions: functional currency measurement, initial recognition at transaction date rate, year-end revaluation of monetary items, recognition of exchange gains/losses in profit or loss, fixed assets at liaison offices recorded at historical cost using average remittance rate, and non-monetary items at historical exchange rates. Section 10 details inventory valuation: cost includes purchases, conversion, and other costs; finished vehicles, spare parts, and work-in-progress at lower of manufacturing cost (weighted average) or net realisable value; stores, packing materials, and tools at lower of weighted average cost or net realisable value; raw materials and components similarly; non-material machinery spares expensed; goods in transit at actual cost; net realisable value defined as estimated selling price less completion and selling costs.

nodes.title: 11 Employee benefits
nodes.summary: This text outlines accounting policies for employee benefits: privilege leave, recognized as a liability when service is rendered, with short-term treatment for leave expected to be used within 12 months, measured at expected cost; gratuity, a defined benefit plan funded through LIC and Bajaj Allianz Life Insurance, with liabilities calculated actuarially using the projected unit credit method, remeasurements in OCI, and net interest cost in profit or loss; and provident fund contributions to the Company's trust, accounted for as a defined benefit plan with expense recognized on service and any deficits recognized as a liability.

nodes.title: 12 Taxation
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting policies: income tax (current tax measured per Income Tax Act 1961 and ICDS; current tax on outside profit/loss items; management evaluation of tax positions; deferred tax on temporary differences, recognition of deferred tax assets, and offsetting), GST/value added taxes on asset acquisition and expenses (net recognition with exceptions, tax recoverable/payable in balance sheet), provisions and contingent liabilities (recognition criteria and disclosure), leases including investment properties (contract assessment, lessee short-term and low-value asset exemptions, lessor operating lease accounting), and government grants and incentives (recognition at fair value, income-related grants deferred, export incentives, and below-market interest loans treated as grants).

nodes.title: Accounting Policies: GST, Provisions, Contingent Liabilities, and Leases
nodes.summary: This page continues the summary of material accounting policies. It first explains GST/value added tax treatment: expenses and assets are recognized net of GST, except when tax is non-recoverable (included in asset cost or expense) or when receivables/payables include tax; net tax recoverable/payable is shown in other current/non-current assets/liabilities. Section 13 covers provisions and contingent liabilities, detailing recognition criteria for provisions (present obligation, probable outflow, reliable estimate) and disclosure requirements for contingent liabilities, with no provision or disclosure for remote outflows. Section 14 addresses leases, including investment properties: lease identification at inception, lessee accounting for short-term and low-value asset leases (exemptions, straight-line expense), and lessor accounting for operating leases (straight-line rental income, initial direct costs added to carrying amount and recognized over lease term).

nodes.title: 15 Government grant and Incentives
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting policies: government grants (recognition at fair value, income-related deferral, export incentives, below-market loans); dividends (provision for declared but undistributed dividends); cash and cash equivalents (definition for cash flow statements); earnings per share (basic and diluted calculations, adjustments for bonus shares); segment reporting (three reportable segments based on product and geography); borrowing costs (expensed, no qualifying assets); and fair value measurement (financial instruments at fair value, principal or advantageous market, market participant assumptions, highest and best use for non-financial assets). It also includes the annual report header and page numbers.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies: Dividends, Cash, EPS, Segments, Borrowing Costs
nodes.summary: The page outlines five accounting policies: Dividends are provisioned when declared and no longer discretionary before period end but unpaid; Cash and cash equivalents include cash on hand and short-term, highly liquid investments with maturities of three months or less, readily convertible and subject to insignificant risk; Earnings per share includes basic EPS calculated by dividing net profit attributable to equity shareholders by the weighted average number of equity shares outstanding, adjusted for events like bonus shares, and diluted EPS adjusted for all dilutive potential equity shares; Segment reporting identifies three reportable segments—Automotive business and Investments and Others—reported consistently with internal reporting to the Core Management Committee, including the Managing Director as Chief Operating Decision Maker, examining performance by product and geography; Borrowing costs are expensed as incurred, with no general or specific borrowing costs directly attributable to qualifying assets during the year.

nodes.title: 21 Fair value measurement
nodes.summary: The text defines fair value measurement for financial instruments, including the price received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants. It specifies that transactions occur in the principal or most advantageous accessible market, using market participant assumptions and considering highest and best use for non-financial assets. The Company uses valuation techniques maximizing observable inputs and categorizes fair value measurements into a three-level hierarchy: Level 1 (quoted prices), Level 2 (observable inputs), and Level 3 (unobservable inputs). It also covers policies for recurring and non-recurring measurements, determination of asset and liability classes, and references to related disclosures on valuation methods, hierarchy, investment properties, and financial instruments.

nodes.title: 22 Other Income
nodes.summary:
22 Other Income
a) Dividends
Dividends are recognised in the Statement of Profit and Loss only when the right to receive payment is established, and it is probable that the economic benefits associated with the dividend will flow to the Company and that the amount of the dividend can be measured reliably.
b) Other income
The Company recognises other income on accrual basis. However, where the ultimate collection of the same lacks reasonable certainty, revenue recognition is postponed to the extent revenue is reasonably certain and can be reliably measured.

nodes.title: 23 Share based payment arrangements
nodes.summary: The text covers four accounting policy notes. Note 23 details employee stock options (ESOPs), including fair value determination, expense recognition over vesting periods, treatment of service, performance, and non-vesting conditions, and dilution effects on EPS. Note 24 describes the ESOP Trust as a vehicle for distributing shares, treating held shares as treasury shares at cost with no gain or loss recognition. Note 25 outlines adjusting and non-adjusting events after the reporting period. Note 26 discusses new and amended standards effective from 1 April 2024 that had no impact, and confirms no early adoption of pending standards.

nodes.title: ESOP Policies, Treasury Shares, and Post-Reporting Events
nodes.summary: The text covers ESOP accounting policies, including treatment of service, performance, market, and non-vesting conditions, expense recognition, and dilution effects. It details treasury shares via an ESOP Trust, recognition at cost, no gain/loss, and settlement of options. Finally, it addresses events after the reporting period, distinguishing adjusting events (adjust amounts) from non-adjusting events (disclose nature and financial effect or state inability to estimate).

nodes.title: Basis of preparation
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Group's material accounting policies, starting with the basis of preparation. It states that financial statements comply with Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) under the Companies Act, 2013, prepared on an accrual and historical cost basis except for certain financial assets and liabilities measured at fair value. Statements are presented in INR (functional currency) rounded to the nearest crore. Assets and liabilities, except deferred tax, are classified as current or non-current based on a 12-month operating cycle; deferred tax items are non-current. The operating cycle is determined as 12 months.

nodes.title: Material accounting policies
nodes.summary: This note outlines material accounting policies for consolidated financial statements. It covers the basis of consolidation, including control definition, subsidiary financial statement alignment, non-controlling interests, acquisitions, dilution, and elimination of intragroup transactions. It details investment in associates using the equity method, covering initial recognition, adjustments for net assets, goodwill, share of profits/losses, OCI, impairment, and loss of significant influence. It also specifies accounting policies for the financial service business, including revenue recognition from contracts with customers (interest income via EIR, fees and commissions, net gain on fair value changes), expenditures (finance costs and fees), and financial assets at amortized cost (amortized cost calculation, SPPI test, and impairment).

nodes.title: Accounting Policies for Financial Services: Revenue and Expenditures
key_items: Net gain on fair value changes
nodes.summary: This page outlines accounting policies for the Group's financial services business, covering revenue recognition and expenditures. It details interest income using the effective interest rate method for financial assets at amortized cost or FVOCI, and contractual interest for FVTPL assets. Fees and commission income are recognized for services, bounce/penal charges, insurance commissions, and loan foreclosure/prepayment. Net gain on fair value changes is recognized on a net basis for FVTPL assets, including realized and unrealized gains/losses. Expenditures include finance costs via the EIR method and fees/commission expenses on an accrual basis. The page begins to address financial assets.

nodes.title: At amortized cost
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting policies for financial instruments: amortized cost, including calculation via effective interest rate (EIR), the SPPI test, and classification of bank balances, loans, trade receivables, and other instruments. It defines amortized cost and covers unamortized transaction income and impairment allowance. For FVTOCI, it details classification, EIR amortization, fair value measurement, and OCI treatment. FVTPL classification and measurement are explained. Impairment using expected credit losses (ECL) is described, including Stage 1 (12-month ECL), Stage 2 (lifetime ECL), Stage 3 (credit-impaired) criteria, write-off policy, and stage 3 classification based on past due status.

nodes.title: Financial Asset Measurement Policies: FVTOCI and FVTPL
key_items: At fair value through Other Comprehensive Income (FVTOCI)
At fair value through profit and loss (FVTPL)
nodes.summary: The page outlines accounting policies for financial assets under FVTOCI and FVTPL. It defines gross carrying amount and notes that unamortized transaction income and impairment allowance are included under 'Loans'. For FVTOCI, assets are measured at fair value with unrealized gains/losses in OCI, EIR amortization and impairment losses in profit and loss, and recycling of OCI gains/losses upon sale. FVTPL classification applies to assets not meeting amortized cost or FVTOCI criteria, or by election to avoid accounting mismatch, with fair value changes recognized in profit and loss.

nodes.title: iv. Impairment of Financial Asset
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting policies for impairment of financial assets and derivative instruments. It details the expected credit loss (ECL) model, categorizing assets into three stages based on credit risk changes: stage 1 (12-month ECL), stage 2 (lifetime ECL for significant credit risk increase), and stage 3 (credit-impaired). It defines criteria for each stage, including days past due and default evidence, and explains ECL measurement using probability of default, loss given default, and exposure at default, adjusted for forward-looking macroeconomic scenarios and time value of money. Write-off and enforcement policies are noted. Separately, it covers derivative financial instruments (CCIRS and IRS) used for hedging interest rate and foreign exchange risk, including initial and subsequent fair value measurement, gain/loss recognition, and cash flow hedge designation.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies for Credit Risk Stages and ECL Measurement
key_items: (c) Without significant increase in credit risk since initial recognition (stage 1)
nodes.summary: The page outlines three accounting policies: (b) Significant increase in credit risk (stage 2), covering assessment at each reporting period, overdue indicators, and PD computation on homogenous portfolios using past trends and future economic conditions; (c) Without significant increase in credit risk since initial recognition (stage 1), recognizing 12-month ECL based on past behavioral trends and statistical analysis; and (d) Measurement of ECL, describing unbiased, probability-weighted estimation incorporating past events, current conditions, forward-looking scenarios, time value of money, and the three components PD, LGD, and EAD, with periodic recalibration.

nodes.title: v. Derivative financial instruments
nodes.summary: The text covers the Company's accounting policies for derivative financial instruments and foreign currencies. It details the use of Cross Currency Interest Rate Swaps and Interest Rate Swaps to manage interest rate and foreign exchange risk, including initial recognition at fair value, subsequent remeasurement, and recognition of gains/losses. It explains hedge accounting, specifically cash flow hedges, including designation, documentation, effectiveness assessment, and accounting treatment of effective portions in OCI and reclassification to profit or loss. It also covers foreign currency translation, including functional currency determination, initial and subsequent measurement of foreign currency transactions, and recognition of exchange differences, with exceptions for net investments in foreign operations.

nodes.title: Hedge Accounting Policies and Foreign Currency Consolidation
nodes.summary: This document outlines the Group's accounting policies for hedge accounting, detailing the formal designation process, documentation requirements, risk management objectives, and ongoing effectiveness assessment. It specifically covers cash flow hedges, including how effective portions of gains or losses are initially recognized in OCI, later reclassified to profit or loss, and treated upon hedge termination or changes in forecast transactions. Additionally, it addresses foreign currency translation, stating that consolidated financial statements are presented in INR, functional currencies are determined for each entity, and the direct method of consolidation is used, with disposal gains or losses reclassified accordingly.

nodes.title: Transactions and balances
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for foreign currency transactions and balances, including initial recognition at spot rates, translation of monetary and non-monetary items, and treatment of exchange differences (in profit or loss, OCI, or as net investment in foreign operations). It details consolidation translation of foreign operations' assets, liabilities, income, and expenses into INR, goodwill and fair value adjustments, and disposal treatment. Taxation policies are outlined for current income tax (measurement, recognition outside P&L, management evaluation) and deferred tax (liability method, recognition criteria, offsetting). It notes that other material accounting policies are similar to the parent's standalone financial statements.

nodes.title: Foreign Currency Translation and Taxation Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: The page covers accounting policies for foreign currency translation and taxation. It details translation of monetary items with tax effects in OCI, non-monetary items at historical or fair value, and consolidation of foreign operations including translation of assets, liabilities, income, and expenses at appropriate rates. Exchange differences are recognized in OCI and recycled to profit or loss on disposal. Goodwill and fair value adjustments are treated as foreign operation assets/liabilities. It also covers current income tax measurement and recognition outside profit or loss, and deferred tax using the liability method with offsetting criteria.

Capital management objectives and regulatory capital adequacy are outlined. Employee benefits are detailed, including funded gratuity schemes, provident fund, and unfunded schemes like compensated absences, with actuarial assumptions and sensitivity analysis. nodes.title: ii) Fair value hierarchy
nodes.summary: This section on fair value hierarchy explains judgments and estimates for determining fair values of financial instruments recognized and measured at fair value or amortized cost with disclosed fair values. It classifies instruments into three levels per accounting standards: Level 1 (quoted prices in active markets), Level 2 (observable market data), and Level 3 (unobservable inputs). Tables present recurring fair value measurements at March 31, 2025, and March 31, 2024, for financial assets/liabilities (investments at FVTPL and FVTOCI, derivatives) and investment property, detailing Level 1, 2, 3, and total values. Valuation techniques include NAV/rates for open-ended mutual funds. Explanations of each level are provided.

nodes.title: Valuation Techniques used to determine fair value
nodes.summary: The text covers notes to consolidated financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025, focusing on fair value measurement and financial risk management. It details recurring fair value measurements at 31 March 2024 for financial assets and liabilities, including financial investments at FVTPL and FVTOCI, derivative assets and liabilities, with breakdowns by Level 1, 2, and 3, and totals. It also presents assets disclosed at fair value, such as investment property, and explains the three-level fair value hierarchy and valuation techniques. Additionally, it provides fair value of financial assets and liabilities measured at amortised cost for 31 March 2025 and 2024, comparing carrying amounts and fair values. Finally, it introduces financial risk management, noting exposure to credit risk, liquidity risk, and market risk, and the use of derivatives for hedging.

nodes.title: Measurement
nodes.summary: The Measurement section covers financial risk management, focusing on credit, liquidity, and market risks. Credit risk details include exposure sources, impairment allowance using ECL and provision matrix, staging classification, collateral types for vehicle finance, impairment assessment of Pierer Bajaj AG, and investment policy credit rating requirements. Liquidity risk discusses principal sources, working capital adequacy, a Board-approved framework with LCR monitored by ALCO, and contractual maturity analysis of financial liabilities. Market risk defines risk from interest rates, foreign exchange, and credit spreads, with tabular exposure breakdown by maturity buckets. The section also outlines management strategies such as counterparty diversification, credit monitoring, HQLA buffers, and the Board's guiding principles for treasury risk identification and hedging.

nodes.title: Measurement (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers financial risk management, detailing measurement and management of credit risk (including cash equivalents, derivatives, trade receivables, default risk, credit ratings, limits, ageing analysis, and default metrics), liquidity risk (maturity analysis, cashflow timing gaps, LCR per RBI guidelines), and market risk (foreign exchange and interest rate risk via sensitivity analysis, forwards, and options). It describes management strategies: counterparty diversification, credit rating monitoring, robust controls, sufficient cash/marketable securities, ALCO reviews, treasury management with HQLA, buffers, long-term funds, and positive asset-liability mismatch. It also notes the Board's guiding principles and treasury's role in identifying, evaluating, and hedging financial risks.

nodes.title: A) Credit risk
key_items: A.2 Classification of financial assets under various stages (of Financial Service Business)
A.3 Impairment assessment of Pierer Bajaj AG (‘PBAG’ or ‘Associate’)
nodes.summary: The text covers credit risk, its sources, and management. It details exposure to derivatives and trade receivables, impairment allowance using a provision matrix with gross carrying amounts, ECL, and net carrying amounts for 2025 and 2024, and a reconciliation of impairment allowance from 2023 to 2025. It also outlines classification of financial assets under Stage 1, 2, and 3 for the financial service business, including term loans and advances to dealers with ECL and net carrying values. Collateral types for two- and three-wheeler finance are described. Additionally, it covers impairment assessment of Pierer Bajaj AG, including the recognized loss, valuation basis, key assumptions, and sensitivity analysis. Finally, it mentions the investment policy for other financial assets with counterparty credit rating requirements.

nodes.title: B) Liquidity risk
nodes.summary: The text covers the Group's liquidity risk management, detailing principal liquidity sources (cash, bank balances, operational cash flows, surplus investments in fixed income securities) and sufficient working capital to meet liabilities, resulting in negligible liquidity risk. It provides a table of net working capital funds for 2025 and 2024. For a subsidiary, it describes a Board-approved Liquidity Risk Management Framework covering policy, strategies, liquidity coverage ratio (LCR), risk measurement (currency and interest rate risk), and monitoring; the subsidiary exceeds LCR requirements and ALCO monitors asset-liability mismatches. It also includes a table summarizing contractual maturities of financial liabilities (non-derivative and derivative) as of March 31, 2025 and 2024.

nodes.title: C) Market risk
nodes.summary: The text is a market risk disclosure comprising a tabular breakdown in Indian crore rupees of exposures across two maturity buckets (up to one year and more than one year) with totals, including line items such as 6,372.71, 3,153.78, 743.57, 10,270.06, 5,580.82, 1,152.57, 597.03, 7,330.42, and additional more-than-one-year and total figures (127.64, 18.56, 125.84, 633.33, 775.23, 759.17, 8,089.59, 16,512.10, 16,530.66).
